section_summaries.epidemiology: Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (AHC) is primarily caused by enterovirus 70 and a variant of coxsackievirus A24, with other enteroviruses and adenoviruses also causing it. The first pandemic of AHC was identified in Ghana in 1969 and spread globally, affecting millions. Enteroviruses causing AHC are highly transmissible, especially in densely populated tropical areas, spreading via ocular/respiratory secretions or contaminated fomites. Epidemics can be explosive, infecting up to 100% of household members and 15% of the general population. Outbreaks can be seasonal, with adolescents and young adults most commonly affected. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD) is most commonly caused by coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus 71, with recent cases and outbreaks also linked to coxsackievirus A6 and A10, and other enteroviruses. HFMD was first described in 1958 and has been reported globally, with enterovirus 71-associated outbreaks frequent in Asia and Australia since the 1990s.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Direct transmission of enterovirus 70 or coxsackievirus A24 from infected hands or fomites to the eye leads to viral replication in the palpebral and bulbar conjunctivae and corneal epithelial cells. Both viruses bind to sialic acid on ocular epithelium, while coxsackievirus A24 can also bind to sialic acid in the respiratory tract. Viral replication in the conjunctivae and cornea causes cell destruction and hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, with an incubation period of 24 to 72 hours. Disease severity varies with the number of infected cells and inflammation. Protective immunity is elicited but immunity to enterovirus 70 wanes within 7 years. The pathogenesis of HFMD is unclear, but fecal-oral transmission is suspected, leading to initial virus replication in the lower gastrointestinal tract, followed by viremia and replication in the oropharynx.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Most enteroviral infections are asymptomatic or associated with non-specific febrile illness, respiratory tract infection (coryza, pharyngitis, pneumonia), or herpangina (oral ulcers). Rare, serious manifestations include neonatal sepsis, meningoencephalitis, myopericarditis, and for enterovirus 71, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage, and cardiopulmonary failure. Chronic infections can occur in immunocompromised individuals. Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis presents with abrupt eye pain, photophobia, eyelid swelling, fever, headache, and pre-auricular lymphadenopathy, with sub-conjunctival hemorrhage being characteristic. Symptoms typically peak on the first day and resolve within days. Children with HFMD usually present with fever, sore throat, and refusal to eat, with vesicles and ulcers on buccal mucosa and tongue, and papules and vesicles with surrounding erythema on the hands, feet, wrists, ankles, buttocks, and genitalia. HFMD caused by enterovirus 71 may rarely lead to severe neurologic complications like aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and acute flaccid paralysis (1.7% case-fatality ratio). Other severe systemic manifestations include acute respiratory disease (especially with enterovirus D68), epidemic pleurodynia, myocarditis, pericarditis, and neonatal infections.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Enterovirus infection should be suspected in persons with hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, or vesicles and papules on the hands, feet, and oropharynx. Diagnosis is typically made on clinical grounds but can be confirmed by cell culture or identification of viral RNA via reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction. The generalized rash of enterovirus infection can resemble measles, rubella, or roseola. Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis can also be caused by other enteroviruses or adenoviruses (type 11) and cannot be clinically distinguished from enterovirus 70 or coxsackievirus A24. HFMD skin lesions may resemble those of herpes simplex virus or varicella-zoster virus infections. Acute flaccid paralysis can be confused with paralytic poliomyelitis, and surveillance commonly detects non-polio enteroviruses.
section_summaries.treatment: No specific therapy for enterovirus infection is recommended, although several drugs are in development. Pleconaril has shown promise in improving survival in neonates with enterovirus sepsis. Intravenous immune globulin has been used to treat severe enteroviral infections, including overwhelming infection in neonates, myocarditis, and meningoencephalitis, but controlled clinical trial data are not available.
section_summaries.prevention: Good hygiene, particularly handwashing, limits fecal-oral or ocular transmission and is the primary method of preventing enterovirus infection. Social distancing measures, such as closing schools, are also used. In December 2015, China's Food and Drug Administration approved two inactivated enterovirus 71 whole-virus vaccines for preventing severe HFMD, with efficacy reported to be approximately 95% or higher in clinical trials.
